anti_overlap: Does not cover per-encounter ceremony weight or catch-event emotional design — that is fd-monster-collection-loop.
Does not cover GPS/real-world session shape and walk-length behavior — that is fd-location-game-ops.
Does not cover dialog ritual structure or narrative tone — that is fd-dialog-ritual-design.
decision_lens: Does this density option treat the walk itself as the game, or does it treat the walk as delivery infrastructure for encounter events?
focus: Slow-game / cozy-game pacing: how density shapes the emotional cadence of a session, the role of empty time, and whether the game sustains grip without a metrics treadmill
name: fd-cozy-game-pacing
persona: Apply the perspective of a cozy/slow-game designer fluent in Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, Spiritfarer, and A Short Hike — they care about whether the negative space between encounters is designed or accidental, measure success by whether a player can have a satisfying session that includes no reward at all, and flag any density setting that fills empty time to prevent boredom rather than to create meaning.
review_areas: Animal Crossing's K.K. Slider Saturdays work because the rest of the week is sparse — the ceremony matters because the calendar is mostly quiet. Assess whether any of the four density options creates a comparable 'most sessions are quiet, some sessions are eventful' cadence, and which option most risks filling every session with content at the cost of making events feel routine.

Option A (guaranteed Unc per lure) guarantees a reward every session, which removes the anticipation arc but also removes the risk of a 'bad walk.' Evaluate the Animal Crossing daily-task design principle: guaranteed low-stakes engagement is a different emotional register than probabilistic high-stakes engagement — and assess which register fits Unc Rancher's aesthetic better.

Stardew Valley's seasonal structure creates natural density inversions (festival days are dense, winter is sparse) that make the dense moments feel earned. Examine whether Unc Rancher's lure mechanic can serve as a player-controlled density dial that achieves the same effect — and whether any of the four options would undermine or support that player agency.

Option D's possibility of getting nothing is the cozy-game 'walk for its own sake' design — the walk has value independent of Unc acquisition. Assess the risk that this framing requires explicit game-language support (tutorial copy, zero-encounter session UI) to land correctly, and whether v0's scope allows that support to be built.

Identify whether any of the proposed options include a mechanism for the walk itself to be legible as progress — distance logged, places visited, lures tried — independent of Unc outcomes. The absence of non-encounter feedback loops is a pacing risk for cozy-game retention that is distinct from metrics-treadmill retention.

Consider the 'lure-duration-gated' alternative raised in the brief (album-length walk → one Unc, film-length walk → more) as a slow-game pattern: it ties encounter density to the player's ambient media engagement rather than to optimization pressure. Evaluate this against the four options on the 'walk as the game' criterion.

severity_examples.condition: If every walk reliably produces 3–4 encounters, players lose the experience of walking without agenda — the game trains attention toward encounter management rather than environmental presence, conflicting with the 'anti-Pokémon-GO maximalism' aesthetic statement.
severity_examples.scenario: Option C fills every walk with content, removing negative space

severity_examples.condition: If the app shows nothing after a 3km lure-walk with no Unc (no distance logged, no lure 'charge' displayed, no world-state feedback), the session feels like a broken app experience rather than a designed 'quiet day' — the empty session must be legible as intentional.
severity_examples.scenario: Option D zero-encounter session with no ambient feedback

severity_examples.condition: After 20 walks, a player who always gets exactly one Unc loses the low-level tension that makes arrival feel like arrival — the walk becomes a commute with a known destination. This is survivable at v0 but becomes a design debt that is expensive to reverse once players have built habits.
severity_examples.scenario: Guaranteed reward (Option A) collapses anticipation arc over time

success_hints: The cozy-game test: can a player have a 'good session' with zero encounters? If yes, the density design is walk-forward. If no, the walk is infrastructure and the game's real loop is encounter collection.

Negative space is not absence of content — it is designed quiet that makes the next event feel like contrast. Identify what event or feedback marks the transition from quiet walk to encounter, and whether that transition is currently designed or incidental.

The lure-duration-gated alternative (brief §2) deserves explicit evaluation against the slow-game criterion — it is the only proposed option that ties encounter density to the player's investment in the ambient media experience rather than to distance optimization.
task_context: Reviewing the four encounter density options (A/B/C/D) for Unc Rancher v0 through a slow-game / cozy-game design lens — assessing whether each density option supports a walk-forward experience with designed negative space, or degrades the walk into a reward-delivery mechanism.
